sampleAnswers.answer:
The Japanese defeat in the Pacific War was the result of material and strategic attrition. American industrial and naval power, which Japan could not match, gradually destroyed Japan's fleet, air power and shipping, and then forced its surrender. Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor in December 1941 brought the United States into the war, but Japan had no realistic plan for a long conflict. The atomic bombings and the Soviet entry into the war in August 1945 shortened the struggle and determined the timing of the surrender, but they did not create the conditions for defeat, which were already in place.

Japan's weaknesses were structural. It lacked oil, iron, rubber and many other resources, and it depended on seizing the Dutch East Indies and other territories whose supply lines were long and vulnerable. American submarines sank a large proportion of Japanese merchant shipping, which cut off the raw materials needed by Japan's factories. Japan could build some warships and aircraft, but it could not replace the pilots and ships it lost at the rate that the United States could replace its own. This imbalance in industrial capacity was the foundation of the Japanese defeat.

The turning points came in 1942 and 1944. The Battle of Midway in June 1942 destroyed four Japanese aircraft carriers and ended Japan's capacity to take the offensive in the central Pacific. The campaign at Guadalcanal, from August 1942 to February 1943, showed that Japanese forces could be beaten on land. From 1943 the United States adopted island hopping, bypassing strongly held islands and seizing bases from which long-range bombers could reach Japan. The Battle of Leyte Gulf in October 1944 destroyed the remaining effective Japanese fleet, and the capture of Saipan brought the Japanese home islands within range of the B-29.

The final phase was marked by costly fighting and by the strategic blockade. The Battle of Okinawa, from April to June 1945, caused very heavy casualties on both sides and convinced many American planners that an invasion of the Japanese home islands would be even costlier. Air raids, including the firebombing of Tokyo in March 1945, destroyed much of Japan's industry and housing. The Potsdam Declaration of July 1945 demanded unconditional surrender, and the Japanese government did not respond in a way that Washington accepted.

The atomic bombs dropped on Hiroshima on 6 August and Nagasaki on 9 August 1945 caused immense destruction and convinced Emperor Hirohito's government that the war could not be won. The Soviet declaration of war on 8 August and the invasion of Manchuria on 9 August removed Japan's hope of a negotiated peace through Moscow. Historians continue to debate whether the bombs or the Soviet entry was more decisive in the surrender, but both accelerated a defeat that the long process of attrition had already made inevitable.

Japanese strategic choices also contributed to the defeat. Japan attacked the United States without a secure path to a negotiated peace, and after Midway it was unable to concentrate its remaining naval forces. Japanese commanders at Guadalcanal, Iwo Jima and Okinawa chose to defend isolated islands to the last man, which inflicted heavy casualties on the Americans but consumed the troops and aircraft that Japan needed for its home defence. Such tactics showed the courage of Japanese soldiers, yet they could not change the underlying balance of resources, and each costly island campaign strengthened the case for continued American pressure.

On balance, the Japanese defeat was caused primarily by American material superiority, which turned a war of resources into one that Japan could not sustain. Naval battles and island campaigns exposed Japan's limits, and the blockade and bombing removed its capacity to recover. The atomic bombs and the Soviet declaration of war determined the timing of the surrender, but they completed a defeat that resource weakness and strategic error had already set in motion.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 21–25 row: it makes a sustained judgement that material attrition caused the Japanese defeat and treats the atomic bombs and the Soviet entry as factors that set the timing, supported by dated evidence such as Midway, Leyte Gulf and Okinawa. To lift it further, examine more closely why Japan's leaders did not surrender before August 1945.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Japan was defeated in the Pacific because the United States was able to outproduce it and to win the battles that decided the war at sea. Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor brought the United States into the war, but Japan did not have the resources to fight a long war. Its navy lost many carriers at the Battle of Midway in 1942, and after that it was on the defensive.

The United States then used island hopping to capture bases close to Japan. Japanese forces were defeated at Guadalcanal and at Leyte Gulf, and American aircraft bombed Japanese cities. Japan also had shortages of oil and other materials, which made it hard to replace its lost ships and planes.

The atomic bombs and the entry of the Soviet Union into the war in August 1945 were the final causes of Japan's surrender. Japan surrendered on 15 August, and the formal surrender took place in September.

The sequence matters. Midway removed Japan's offensive capacity, while the island campaigns and the submarine blockade meant that Japan could not reinforce its remaining positions. The bombings and the Soviet entry were important, but they came after the material decline that had already made defeat certain. Japanese leaders hoped to negotiate through Moscow until August 1945, which shows how far the strategic situation had deteriorated. A stronger answer would make this sequence the basis of its judgement.

To reach 16–20, weigh the material causes against the final events and explain why the atomic bombs and the Soviet entry mattered at this stage.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The Allied occupation of Japan was largely successful in its core aims of demilitarisation and democratisation, but it was less successful in securing full accountability for the war and it was reshaped by the Cold War. The occupation changed Japan's political and economic structures, yet several of its aims were compromised by American priorities. The judgement of this answer is that the occupation succeeded in transforming Japan into a stable, non-militaristic state, but it fell short of its wider goal of a complete break with the past.

Demilitarisation was achieved quickly. The Japanese army and navy were dismantled under General Douglas MacArthur, the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, and the new constitution of 1947 renounced war as a sovereign right and forbade the maintenance of armed forces with war potential in Article 9. This was a radical change for a country whose militarism had shaped its foreign policy for decades. The occupation also dismantled the zaibatsu industrial combines, which concentrated economic power, and it introduced land reform that broke up many large estates.

Democratisation was equally visible. The new constitution made the Diet the centre of government, granted civil liberties and gave women the vote, and the first elections in which women voted were held in April 1946. Trade unions were legalised and encouraged, and education was reorganised to remove militarist teaching. These reforms built the institutions of a democratic state, and they lasted long after the occupation ended. In this sense the occupation achieved its aim of creating a Japan that could govern itself peacefully.

Accountability was a more limited success. The International Military Tribunal for the Far East tried leading figures from 1946, and seven men were hanged in December 1948. However, the Emperor was not tried, and his renunciation of divinity in January 1946 did not bring him to trial. MacArthur judged that retaining the Emperor would help stability and make the occupation easier to run. Some accused war criminals, including Kishi Nobusuke, were released without trial. The Emperor's retention and these releases show that the aim of full accountability was sacrificed to practical goals.

The Cold War changed the occupation's priorities. From 1947 to 1948 the United States began a reverse course, which emphasised economic recovery and anti-communism rather than punishment. Japan was seen as a bulwark against communism in East Asia, and the Korean War of 1950 boosted Japanese industry through American orders. Communists were purged from public employment, and the National Police Reserve created in 1950 became Japan’s SDF in 1954. Demilitarisation was therefore weakened by the Cold War, even though the constitution still limited Japan's military.

The occupation formally ended with the Treaty of San Francisco in 1951, which restored Japanese sovereignty, but it was accompanied by a security treaty that allowed American bases to remain. This outcome shows that the occupation achieved some of its aims in a changed form. The United States had a stable and democratic ally, yet Japan remained dependent on American security.

Economic reform also met part of its aim. The dissolution of the zaibatsu and the Antimonopoly Law of 1947 weakened the largest industrial combines, although many of their business networks later re-formed as the keiretsu groups of the 1950s. Land reform from 1946 transferred much farmland to former tenants, creating a more equal rural society that supported stability and conservative politics. These changes lasted, which shows that the occupation's economic aims were achieved more fully than its political ones.

In conclusion, the Allied occupation achieved its central aims of demilitarisation and democratisation, and it left Japan with institutions that sustained peace and growth. However, its aim of full accountability was compromised by the decision not to try the Emperor and by the early release of some accused leaders. Cold War priorities then shifted the purpose of the occupation towards a stable ally. The occupation was therefore successful in its core reforms, but it was not a complete break with the past.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 21–25 row: a clear judgement that separates the achieved aims from the compromised ones, supported by specific reforms, trials and the reverse course. It would lift further by weighing the Emperor's retention more carefully against the stability it was meant to protect.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The Allied occupation of Japan achieved many of its aims. The Japanese army and navy were dismantled, and General Douglas MacArthur oversaw a new constitution in 1947 that renounced war. Land reform broke up large estates, and the zaibatsu were broken up. Democracy was strengthened by elections in which women voted for the first time in 1946, and by the legal recognition of trade unions.

The occupation was less successful in ensuring accountability for the war. Leading war criminals were tried in Tokyo and seven were hanged in 1948, but the Emperor was not tried. Some accused figures were released without trial. The Cold War also changed American priorities, so that from 1947 the United States wanted Japan to be a stable ally against communism rather than a country that had been punished.

The occupation's reforms depended on Japanese cooperation. The Japanese government accepted most of SCAP's directives, and the Emperor's support helped make changes acceptable to many Japanese. The occupation worked through existing institutions, which speeded reform but also allowed some wartime officials to return to influence.

The occupation was successful in its reforms, but its aim of a complete break with the past was compromised by American priorities.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 11–15 row: a structured response that describes the reforms and the trials, with some implied judgement about the limits of success. It would lift by stating a clear judgement and explaining why the Cold War changed the occupation's aims.

sampleAnswers.answer: The occupation aimed to demilitarise Japan and make it democratic. MacArthur oversaw a new constitution in 1947 and women were given the vote. The Emperor stayed on the throne and was not tried for war crimes. Japan became an ally of the United States after the occupation ended in 1951. The Emperor was retained and many accused leaders were released, so accountability was limited, although demilitarisation and democratisation were firmly established.

The statement is largely accurate. The War Crimes Tribunals did deliver some justice, but Allied interests shaped who was tried, what was punished and how long the process lasted. The Tokyo Tribunal, in particular, reflected the priorities of the United States, which wanted to secure Japan as an ally against communism. The omission of the Emperor, and the limits placed on the trials, show that Allied interests shaped the outcome more than a commitment to justice alone. The Allied occupation of Japan, which lasted until 1952, gave the Americans the power to decide these matters.

The Tokyo Tribunal, formally the International Military Tribunal for the Far East, was established in 1946 under General Douglas MacArthur, the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers. It tried senior Japanese military and political leaders for crimes against peace, conventional war crimes and crimes against humanity. Its judgements included the execution of General Tojo Hideki and other leaders. In this sense, the tribunal delivered justice for crimes such as the Nanking Massacre and the treatment of prisoners of war.

However, the tribunal was shaped by Allied interests. The Emperor Hirohito was not prosecuted, because the United States believed that his cooperation would help the occupation run smoothly and that his removal could provoke unrest. The decision protected a figure who had been central to the war, and it reflected the American wish to use the existing Japanese government as a means of reform. Many lower-ranking figures, including those responsible for biological and chemical experiments, were protected in return for their data or were never charged.

Allied interests changed further as the Cold War developed. By 1948 the United States had begun the reverse course, which shifted priority from punishment and demilitarisation to rebuilding Japan as a bulwark against communism in East Asia. The end of the trials and the release of some accused figures in the late 1940s followed this change, and they showed that the justice of the process was subordinate to strategic needs.

The Nuremberg Trials, by contrast, were broader in their aims and more closely tied to the principles of international law. They established the principle that individuals could be held responsible for crimes against peace and humanity. Yet even Nuremberg reflected the interests of the victorious powers, because the Soviet Union and the Western Allies applied the law selectively and excluded the crimes of their own forces.

The justice of the process was also weakened by the conduct of the victors. The Soviet Union sat as a prosecuting power at both Nuremberg and Tokyo, yet the Katyn massacre of Polish officers was not included in the charges against the German defendants, and in 1949 the Soviet Union held its own trial at Khabarovsk of Japanese personnel charged with bacteriological warfare. The Indian judge Radhabinod Pal dissented from the Tokyo judgement, arguing that the trial applied law retrospectively and reflected the power of the victors. His dissent shows that contemporaries questioned whether the process was justice at all, rather than the exercise of Allied power. His point was reinforced by the fact that neither tribunal examined the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, so the most destructive acts of the war were excluded from judgement.

Overall, the War Crimes Tribunals did achieve a measure of justice in holding leaders accountable for atrocities. But their outcomes, particularly in Tokyo, show that Allied interests determined who was tried, who was spared and when the process ended. The statement is therefore largely accurate, although justice was not entirely absent.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Ideology was the more significant influence on the policies of the Cold War, although economic and political concerns determined how those policies were carried out. Marxist-Leninist ideology gave the Soviet leadership a conviction that capitalist states were hostile, and American leaders responded with a belief that communist expansion had to be contained. These beliefs framed the conflict from its beginning. However, the most important policies, such as the Marshall Plan and the defence of Western Europe, were shaped by practical concerns about security, economic recovery and the political stability of allies.

Ideology established the terms of the conflict. The Soviet Union's postwar control of Eastern Europe was justified by a Marxist-Leninist view of history, and Stalin's distrust of the West was rooted in a belief that capitalist powers would eventually attack the socialist camp. In the United States, George Kennan's Long Telegram of February 1946 described Soviet power as an expansionist force driven by ideology, and the Truman Doctrine of March 1947 committed the United States to supporting states resisting communist pressure. Containment rested on the assumption that communism was a monolithic threat, which was an ideological judgement rather than a purely strategic one.

Economic and political concerns, however, determined the form of American policy. The Marshall Plan, announced in June 1947, was designed to restore European economies, create markets for American goods and prevent the political instability that might bring communist parties to power. Its aims were economic and political, and it did not require the United States to accept Soviet ideology as a threat in every sphere. Similarly, the creation of NATO in 1949 responded to the security needs of Western Europe after the Berlin blockade, rather than to any conviction that communism could be defeated by military means alone.

Soviet policy was also shaped by economic and political concerns. Devastated by the Second World War, the Soviet Union needed to rebuild, to secure its western frontier and to control the governments of Eastern Europe. The consolidation of communist regimes after 1947 and the coup in Czechoslovakia in February 1948 reflected a determination to prevent a hostile government on the Soviet border. These were realist concerns as much as ideological ones, and they explain why Stalin accepted limits on expansion in some areas.

The argument that ideology was more significant rests on its role as the framework within which the superpowers understood each other. Ideology made compromise difficult and made each side read the other's actions as evidence of hostile intent. Yet ideology alone cannot explain the specific policies of the early Cold War. The decision to fight in Korea, to rearm West Germany and to build the Atlantic alliance was driven by strategic and economic calculation as much as by belief.

Later developments test the argument. Eisenhower's New Look relied on nuclear deterrence to contain the Soviet Union more cheaply, which reflected economic concern about the cost of conventional rearmament. The Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962 turned on the strategic need to avoid nuclear war as much as on ideological hostility, and the Soviet withdrawal of its missiles reflected practical considerations. Ideology continued to shape rhetoric, as Ronald Reagan's description of the Soviet Union as an 'evil empire' in 1983 showed, but the policies that eventually ended the conflict owed more to economic pressure and to changes within the Soviet Union.

On balance, ideology was the more significant influence on the broad direction of Cold War policy, because it made a long rivalry seem inevitable and because it shaped how each superpower interpreted the other's motives. Economic and political concerns, however, were more significant in determining the particular policies that were adopted. The Cold War was therefore shaped by ideological conviction working through practical interests, and the most important decisions reflected both.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 21–25 row: it makes a sustained judgement that ideology set the direction of policy while economic and political concerns shaped its form, supported by specific evidence such as the Long Telegram, the Truman Doctrine and the Marshall Plan. To lift it further, weigh more fully the role of the Soviet need for security in the early postwar years.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Ideology shaped the Cold War because the United States and the Soviet Union had opposing views of how society should be organised. The Soviet Union was communist, and the United States believed in capitalism and democracy. This meant each side saw the other as a threat, and the leaders believed the other would try to expand their system.

Economic and political concerns were also important. The United States gave money to Europe through the Marshall Plan to help the economies recover, and it wanted to stop communist parties from winning elections in France and Italy. The Soviet Union wanted security after the war, and it kept control of Eastern Europe to protect its border.

Both ideology and practical concerns influenced policy. Ideology made the conflict seem serious, while economic and political interests decided the specific actions that the superpowers took.

The early Cold War supports both sides of the argument. The Truman Doctrine was a statement of ideological principle, which committed the United States to supporting governments resisting communist pressure, while the Marshall Plan was an economic programme designed to restore markets and political stability in Western Europe. A strong answer would show that the two were linked, because economic recovery was seen as a barrier to communist success. The Soviet imposition of communist governments in Eastern Europe similarly reflected both ideological commitment and the security needs of the state.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Conflict emerged between the United States and the Soviet Union from 1945 because the wartime alliance against Germany rested on shared danger rather than shared aims. The two superpowers had very different visions of the postwar world. The United States, with its economic strength and a monopoly of the atomic bomb from 1945, sought open markets, self-determination and a world order that favoured capitalism. The Soviet Union, which had lost tens of millions of people in the war, wanted secure borders and a buffer of friendly governments in Eastern Europe. Ideology reinforced these differences: each power believed its system was superior and that the other threatened it.

The decisions made at Yalta and Potsdam in 1945 showed the strains. Agreements on Poland and the future of Germany were vague, and the Soviet Union installed communist governments in the countries its army occupied in Eastern Europe. In a speech at Fulton, Missouri, in March 1946, Winston Churchill spoke of an ‘iron curtain’ dividing Europe, and the phrase came to describe the division between the two blocs. George Kennan’s analysis of Soviet behaviour underpinned a policy of containment, which the Truman Doctrine of March 1947 turned into a commitment to support governments resisting communist pressure in Greece and Turkey.

Economic policy deepened the divide. The Marshall Plan of 1948 offered American aid to rebuild Western Europe, and the Soviet Union and its satellites refused to take part. The aid helped to restore Western economies, but Stalin saw it as a means of tying Western Europe to the United States. The Soviet response was the Berlin Blockade of June 1948 to May 1949, in which the Soviet Union cut road and rail access to the Western sectors of the city. The Western powers countered with an airlift that kept West Berlin supplied, and the crisis hardened the division of Germany into two states.

Military alliances followed. The North Atlantic Treaty Organisation was formed in 1949, and the Soviet Union created the Warsaw Pact in 1955 in response to West German rearmament. Each superpower built up its nuclear arsenal, and the Soviet Union tested its own atomic bomb in 1949. The Korean War of 1950 to 1953 showed that the rivalry could become a shooting war, even though neither superpower fought the other directly. The conflict was also fought through proxy states and in the developing world, where both sides competed for influence.

Historians differ on the origins of the Cold War. Orthodox historians place primary responsibility on Soviet expansion in Eastern Europe, while revisionist historians emphasise American economic ambitions and the fear of Soviet power. Post-revisionist scholars argue that both sides misread each other and that their mutual suspicion, combined with domestic politics and the lack of trust after the war, produced an escalating spiral. The best explanation combines these factors: ideological conviction, security fears and economic interests interacted to make conflict almost inevitable.

The rivalry was also shaped by the nuclear dimension. The United States held a monopoly of the atomic bomb until the Soviet test of 1949, and this monopoly shaped American confidence and Soviet anxiety. Once the Soviet Union had its own bomb, both sides began to plan for nuclear confrontation. Neither side was willing to accept the other’s sphere of influence, and each interpreted the other’s actions as an attempt to expand.

In conclusion, conflict emerged between the superpowers from 1945 because their alliance had been temporary, their ideologies were opposed and each feared the other’s power in Europe. The division of Germany, the Iron Curtain and the military blocs made the Cold War a lasting structure rather than a passing dispute.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 21–25 row: the answer makes a sustained judgement about the combination of ideology, security and economic interests, and it uses a wide range of dated evidence. To go further, it could test the historiographical positions more directly against the evidence.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Conflict between the superpowers emerged from 1945 because the wartime alliance against Germany could not survive the postwar settlement. The United States and the Soviet Union had different aims for Europe. The Americans wanted open markets and free elections, while the Soviet Union wanted friendly governments on its western border after the damage it had suffered in the war. Ideology made each side suspicious of the other, and neither trusted the other’s intentions in Germany or Eastern Europe.

The division of Europe became clear in 1946 and 1947. Churchill’s ‘iron curtain’ speech described the split, and the Truman Doctrine committed the United States to resisting communist pressure in Greece and Turkey. The Marshall Plan offered aid to Western Europe, but the Soviet Union refused it and did not allow its satellites to take part. Soon after, the Berlin Blockade showed how far the two sides were willing to go, and it was followed by the creation of NATO in 1949.

The Korean War of 1950 to 1953 showed that the rivalry could turn into a hot war, and both sides built up their nuclear forces. The superpowers were rivals for influence across the world, which made conflict a feature of the postwar years rather than a brief dispute over Europe.

The division of Europe also created a rivalry over the future of Germany. The Soviet Union wanted reparations and a weak Germany, while the Western powers came to see West German recovery as essential to Europe’s prosperity. Each side read the other’s German policy as proof of its aims, and the conflict was fought over Berlin as well as over ideology. By 1955 the division was institutionalised in two alliance systems facing each other across Europe.

Conflict between the superpowers began in 1945 because the United States and the Soviet Union wanted different things from Europe. The Soviet Union took control of Eastern Europe, and the United States responded with the Truman Doctrine.

The rivalry grew because each superpower read the other’s actions as aggressive. Soviet control of Eastern Europe alarmed the West, while American aid and alliances alarmed Moscow, and this mutual fear made the conflict hard to end.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Containment shaped the Cold War more than any other single doctrine, because it defined American policy from the late 1940s onwards and set the framework for alliances, military spending and regional interventions. Its impact was greatest in the decades from 1947 to the 1960s, when it committed the United States to resist Soviet expansion across the world. However, containment also contributed to the rivalry it sought to manage. Its success was real but ambiguous. It helped to contain Soviet expansion in Western Europe, while producing costly interventions and an arms race, and the end of the Cold War owed more to internal Soviet weakness than to containment alone.

The doctrine emerged from the crisis of 1946 to 1947. George Kennan's Long Telegram of 1946 and his article in Foreign Affairs in 1947 argued that the Soviet Union would keep expanding unless it met firm and sustained resistance. The Truman Doctrine of March 1947 pledged US aid to Greece and Turkey, and the Marshall Plan of 1948 provided economic support for Western Europe. These measures made containment the basis of US policy and tied it to economic recovery as well as military power. The creation of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) in 1949 then turned containment into a military alliance, with the United States committed to the defence of Western Europe.

Containment had a lasting effect on military strategy. The National Security Council's report NSC-68 of 1950 called for a major increase in US military spending, and the Korean War of 1950 to 1953 showed the doctrine in action, as the United States resisted communist aggression in Asia. The domino theory, which held that the fall of one state would lead to the fall of its neighbours, justified the expansion of US involvement in Vietnam from the 1950s. Containment therefore gave the United States a reason to build alliances and bases across the world, even where the strategic value of the territory was limited.

Containment also helped to create the conflict it was meant to manage. The Soviet Union responded to the American alliance system by forming the Warsaw Pact in 1955, and both sides built nuclear arsenals in an arms race that brought the world close to catastrophe in the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962. Containment's broader logic, which treated every communist movement as a threat, also led to costly interventions. The Vietnam War was the clearest example, as a commitment that began as containment became a war that cost the United States heavily and divided American society.

The doctrine was adapted over time. Under Richard Nixon and Henry Kissinger, containment was pursued through détente, which combined arms control and trade with the Soviet Union in an effort to manage the rivalry rather than win it outright. Ronald Reagan's Strategic Defense Initiative of 1983 and his military build-up marked a return to pressure on the Soviet Union, which many historians consider a significant factor in the Soviet collapse. Containment was therefore a flexible strategy that changed its methods while keeping the goal of limiting Soviet influence.

The Soviet collapse between 1989 and 1991 seemed to vindicate containment, because the United States had outlasted its rival. Yet the collapse also reflected the internal weaknesses of the Soviet economy, which were exposed by Mikhail Gorbachev's reforms, and the rising costs of the arms race and the war in Afghanistan. Containment's impact on this outcome was therefore indirect. It maintained the pressure, but the decisive factors lay within the Soviet system.

In conclusion, containment shaped the Cold War by defining US foreign policy, building the alliance system and justifying the commitment to resist communism in every region. Its impact was greatest in the first two decades, when it set the structure of the conflict. Its longer-term impact was more mixed, because it helped produce costly wars and an arms race. Containment's strongest claim is that it kept the pressure on the Soviet Union until internal weakness brought the rival down, although its role in that outcome was not decisive on its own.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 21–25 row with a sustained judgement that containment shaped the Cold War's structure and costs, and that its role in the Soviet collapse was indirect. The answer ties the Truman Doctrine, the Marshall Plan, NATO and the domino theory to specific consequences, and weighs them against the Korean War and the arms race. A top answer would show more clearly how far the Vietnam War was a product of containment rather than of the domino theory alone.

sampleAnswers.answer: Containment was the central American policy of the Cold War. It was set out in the Truman Doctrine of 1947, which offered aid to Greece and Turkey to resist communist pressure. The Marshall Plan of 1948 gave economic support to Western Europe, and NATO was formed in 1949 as a military alliance to defend it. Containment was also used in Asia, most clearly in the Korean War from 1950 to 1953. The domino theory then led the United States into Vietnam, where the policy cost many lives. Containment therefore shaped the conflict for four decades. It kept the Soviet Union from expanding into Western Europe, but it also helped to produce an arms race and costly wars. The Soviet collapse in 1991 showed that the policy had succeeded in the end.

The judgement on the Soviet collapse is implied rather than argued. To lift it, weigh containment's early successes against its later costs and state a clear view on its role in 1989 to 1991.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Cold War crises changed relationships between the superpowers in a limited but real way. They produced new mechanisms for managing rivalry, such as the hotline and the Partial Test Ban Treaty, and they showed that direct confrontation carried unacceptable risks. Yet the crises also deepened mutual distrust, and by 1968 the Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia showed that the Soviet Union would still use force to hold its bloc together. The judgement is that the crises moved the superpowers towards managed rivalry rather than resolution, and that the change was real but bounded.

The early crises set the pattern. The Berlin Blockade of 1948 to 1949 was answered by the Berlin airlift and it hardened the division of Germany. The Korean War of 1950 to 1953 showed that the superpowers would fight through proxies, and it led the United States to rearm and to commit to containment in Europe. The Soviet suppression of the Hungarian uprising in 1956 confirmed that the Soviet bloc would be held by force. In each case the superpowers clarified their spheres of influence, and the rivalry became more stable, though more dangerous, because each side now knew the other's red lines.

The most dangerous crisis came in October 1962. Soviet missiles placed in Cuba led to a confrontation between Kennedy and Khrushchev, and the world came close to nuclear war. The settlement, in which the Soviet Union removed its missiles and the United States pledged not to invade Cuba and removed missiles from Turkey, changed the relationship. A hotline between Moscow and Washington was established in 1963 so that leaders could communicate in a future crisis. The superpowers had seen the cost of confrontation, and this shaped their behaviour.

The Berlin Wall, built in August 1961, was a crisis of a different kind. It ended the flow of refugees from East to West and was accepted by the United States, which showed that the superpowers would not risk war over the division of Berlin. This acceptance confirmed the division of Europe and showed that the superpowers had come to treat their spheres of influence as fixed. The change was therefore one of recognition rather than of conflict resolution.

The crises also produced agreements. The Partial Test Ban Treaty of 1963 banned nuclear tests in the atmosphere, in outer space and underwater, and it reflected a shared fear of the dangers of nuclear fallout. It was the first arms control agreement of the Cold War and showed that cooperation was possible when the risks were clear. Even so, the agreement did not stop the arms race, and both sides continued to build up their nuclear arsenals.

The Prague Spring of 1968 tested whether the superpowers had moved beyond confrontation. Alexander Dubcek's programme of reform in Czechoslovakia led to a Soviet-led invasion in August 1968, which ended the reforms. The United States protested but did not intervene, because the superpowers had accepted the division of Europe. This demonstrated the limits of change: the relationship had become more stable, but it still rested on Soviet control of Eastern Europe and on American acceptance of that control.

The Berlin ultimatum of 1958, in which Khrushchev demanded that the Western powers withdraw from West Berlin, ended in stalemate, and the Berlin Wall followed three years later. The superpowers therefore learned that a crisis could be contained without war, but that each side would defend its key interests with force if necessary. This lesson shaped every later crisis, including the Cuban Missile Crisis, and it limited the change that the crises could produce.

In conclusion, Cold War crises changed relationships between the superpowers by producing rules for managing rivalry and by making direct confrontation seem too dangerous. The hotline, the Test Ban Treaty and the acceptance of the Berlin Wall show a move towards stability. However, the Prague Spring confirmed that the rivalry had not ended, and the superpowers still competed through their spheres of influence. By 1968 the change was real but bounded.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Schlesinger’s view accurately describes the danger of the Cuban Missile Crisis, but it overstates its significance as the turning point of the Cold War. The crisis was the closest the superpowers came to nuclear war, and it reshaped how both sides managed their rivalry. However, its long-term effects were shaped by the broader development of arms control and détente, which followed from the shared fear the crisis created. The crisis was therefore significant, but Schlesinger’s emphasis on it as the defining moment underestimates the wider processes of the Cold War.

The danger that Schlesinger describes was real. In October 1962 American reconnaissance revealed Soviet medium-range missiles in Cuba. President Kennedy responded with a naval quarantine and an ultimatum, and for thirteen days the two superpowers moved towards a confrontation that could have led to nuclear war. Military leaders on both sides were prepared for action, and the risk of miscalculation was high. In this sense, Schlesinger’s view is accurate about the immediate significance of the crisis.

The danger was also greater than the diplomatic record suggests. On 27 October 1962 a Soviet submarine, B-59, which was under attack from American destroyers, had its nuclear torpedo readied for launch. The authorisation of three senior officers was required, and one of them, Vasili Arkhipov, refused. The incident shows that the crisis came close to war through decisions that the leaders in Washington and Moscow did not control, and this supports Schlesinger’s point about how close the superpowers came.

The crisis changed the relationship between the superpowers. Khrushchev agreed to withdraw the missiles, and Kennedy pledged not to invade Cuba, and a secret understanding also led to the removal of American missiles from Turkey. The settlement showed both leaders that the risk of nuclear war was too great to accept. A hotline between Washington and Moscow was established in 1963, which provided a direct channel for crisis communication.

The crisis also strengthened the case for arms control. The Partial Test Ban Treaty of 1963 was signed in the aftermath of the crisis, and it banned nuclear tests in the atmosphere, in outer space and underwater. This reflected a shared recognition that the arms race had to be restrained. The treaty did not end the Cold War, but it set a pattern of negotiation that continued with the Non-Proliferation Treaty of 1968 and the SALT talks.

The crisis also had a lasting effect on the Soviet Union. Khrushchev’s withdrawal was seen in Moscow as a humiliation, and it was among the pressures that led to his removal in October 1964. The leadership that followed committed itself to a major build-up of strategic forces in the late 1960s, which aimed to end the American nuclear advantage that the crisis had exposed. The crisis therefore encouraged both restraint and a more determined competition in weapons, and the arms race did not end with the settlement of 1962.

However, Schlesinger’s view overstates the crisis as a turning point. The Berlin crisis of 1961, the Korean War and the arms race had already shaped the Cold War, and the rivalry continued after 1962 with the Vietnam War and the expansion of nuclear arsenals. The crisis did not change the basic ideological and strategic competition between the superpowers. Rather, it reinforced the need for management, not the end of rivalry.

Overall, Schlesinger’s view accurately describes the immediate danger of the crisis and the lessons that leaders drew from it. But the crisis was one stage in a longer contest. Its significance lay in encouraging restraint and negotiation, and this helped to shape the era of détente. The statement is therefore accurate in part, because the crisis was significant but was not the defining moment of the Cold War.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The Berlin crises were significant in changing US–Soviet relations, but their main effect was to harden the division of Europe and to teach both superpowers how to manage a confrontation. The crises did not by themselves transform the relationship, which was shaped more decisively by the nuclear balance and by the Cuban Missile Crisis. Berlin was the most dangerous point of contact in Europe, and each crisis forced the superpowers to consider the risk of war, which led to the first attempts at crisis management.

The first crisis, the Berlin Blockade, came in 1948, when Stalin blocked land access to West Berlin in an attempt to force the Western powers out of the city. The Western Allies responded with the Berlin Airlift, which flew over two million tonnes of supplies into the city until the blockade was lifted in May 1949. The crisis had lasting consequences. It hardened the division of Germany, with the creation of the Federal Republic in 1949 and the German Democratic Republic later that year, and it strengthened the commitment to NATO, which was founded in the same year.

The second crisis began in 1958, when Khrushchev issued the Berlin Ultimatum, demanding that the Western powers withdraw from West Berlin within six months. Eisenhower refused to negotiate under threat, and the crisis was eased by diplomacy, including a summit at Camp David in 1959. The summit in Paris in 1960 collapsed after the U-2 incident over the Soviet Union, which showed that the crisis had damaged trust rather than settling the issue. The Berlin Ultimatum therefore changed relations by revealing how little room the two sides had for compromise on Germany.

The third and most decisive crisis came in 1961. At the Vienna summit in June, Khrushchev pressed Kennedy hard over Berlin, and the Soviet leader believed that the young president was weak. The Berlin Wall, built in August 1961, sealed the boundary between East and West Berlin. The United States did not contest the Wall, and Kennedy accepted it as an end to the flow of refugees from the East. The Wall reduced the tension because it stabilised the division, and this reduced the pressure for a further confrontation over the city.

The Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962 had a greater impact on US–Soviet relations, although Berlin was part of the background. Khrushchev had hoped that Soviet missiles in Cuba would offset the American position in Berlin. The crisis ended with a US promise not to invade Cuba and a secret agreement to remove US missiles from Turkey, and it led to the Moscow–Washington hotline and the Partial Test Ban Treaty of 1963. These arrangements were the most important changes in US–Soviet relations, and they were built on the experience of the Berlin crises.

The Berlin question continued to shape relations into the 1970s. The Quadripartite Agreement of 1971 reduced the risk of confrontation over access to the city, and it became part of the wider détente between Nixon and Brezhnev. This suggests that the Berlin crises contributed to a more stable relationship, because they showed both sides the costs of confrontation. Yet the agreement came only after two decades of crises, and it reflected the acceptance of a divided Berlin rather than a settlement.

In conclusion, the Berlin crises were significant in changing US–Soviet relations because they hardened division and forced the superpowers towards crisis management. Their impact was most visible in the Berlin Blockade and the Berlin Wall, which settled the German question for a generation. The crises were not, however, the decisive factor in changing relations. The Cuban Missile Crisis and the nuclear balance were more important in producing the hotline, the test ban and détente, and Berlin's significance lay in revealing the dangers that shaped them.

The Cuban Missile Crisis in 1962 then brought the superpowers closest to war, and afterwards the hotline and the test ban treaty were agreed. The Berlin crises showed both sides the dangers of confrontation, but they did not change the relationship by themselves, and the Cuban Missile Crisis was more significant for later agreements.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The arms race and the space race both intensified superpower rivalry up to 1968, but they did so in different ways. The arms race made the confrontation dangerous, because nuclear deterrence required each side to match the other's weapons. The space race mainly added prestige and propaganda to a rivalry that was already entrenched. On balance, the arms race contributed far more to the rivalry, although the space race shaped how it was fought and how it was perceived.

The American atomic monopoly ended when the Soviet Union tested a bomb in August 1949, and the arms race escalated when both sides developed thermonuclear weapons, with the United States testing its first hydrogen device in 1952 and the Soviet Union following in 1953. Deterrence depended on each side believing the other could retaliate, which encouraged intercontinental missiles, submarines and larger stockpiles. The most dangerous moment came in October 1962, when the Soviet Union placed nuclear missiles in Cuba and the United States imposed a naval quarantine. The crisis showed how the arms race could bring the superpowers to the brink, and it led directly to a hotline between Washington and Moscow and to the Partial Test Ban Treaty of 1963.

The space race was driven by the same rivalry but added a different dimension. The Soviet launch of Sputnik in October 1957 shocked the United States, which feared that its missile programme was falling behind, and the resulting 'missile gap' debate increased defence spending and led to the creation of NASA in 1958. Soviet achievements continued with Yuri Gagarin's orbital flight in April 1961, and President Kennedy responded by committing the United States to land a man on the Moon before the end of the decade. The space race had direct military value, because the rockets that launched satellites could also carry nuclear warheads, and it gave both sides a platform to claim technological and ideological superiority before the world.

The two races interacted. Sputnik and the missile gap were used to justify larger defence budgets, while Soviet space achievements were presented as proof that communism could outperform capitalism. Success in one field therefore fed confidence in the other, and it encouraged the perception that the Soviet Union might gain a decisive military advantage. The arms race was nonetheless the more dangerous element, because it created the capacity to destroy the other side, while the space race was largely a contest for prestige.

Some historians argue that the space race was equally important, because it shaped American perceptions of Soviet strength and fuelled the sense of crisis that drove the arms race. This view has force, since the missile gap was later shown to be largely unfounded and the space race helped create the political climate for defence spending. Yet the arms race had its own momentum from 1945, and the American nuclear arsenal was growing well before Sputnik. The restraint that followed the crises, including the Partial Test Ban Treaty and the Non-Proliferation Treaty of 1968, shows that the arms race could also produce agreements that limited rivalry.

On balance, the arms race contributed to superpower rivalry to a very great extent, because it made deterrence the basis of superpower relations and gave each side reason to fear the other's next weapon. The space race contributed to a lesser but real extent, by heightening prestige and public anxiety. Together they sustained the rivalry up to 1968 while also producing the early agreements that tried to contain it. The rivalry was driven by the arms race, but the space race made it visible to the world.

Both sides then built more weapons, and this made each side feel threatened by the other. The Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962 showed how dangerous the arms race had become, because the two countries came close to nuclear war.

The space race was also important. In 1957 the Soviet Union launched Sputnik, and this shocked the Americans. They believed the Soviet Union had a lead in missiles, and this made the United States spend more money on defence and science. In 1961 the Soviet Union sent Yuri Gagarin into space, and President Kennedy promised to send an American to the Moon. The space race was a contest between the two systems, and each side wanted to show that its system was better.

Both races made the rivalry stronger. The arms race made the superpowers fear each other, and the space race made the rivalry more public. People around the world watched the space programmes, which made the competition seem very important. The space race therefore contributed to the rivalry in its own way, even though it was not as dangerous as the arms race.

However, there were some attempts to reduce tensions. In 1963 the superpowers signed a treaty banning nuclear tests in the atmosphere, and in 1968 the Non-Proliferation Treaty was agreed. These agreements show that the arms race was not the only thing going on, and that the superpowers could cooperate at times.

Overall, both the arms race and the space race contributed to superpower rivalry. The arms race was probably more important because it was about nuclear weapons and the risk of war, but the space race also mattered because it was a visible contest that the public could follow.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The arms race shaped the Cold War from 1962 to 1991 by making the superpower rivalry more dangerous and by forcing both sides to seek limits on their weapons. It created a deterrence relationship that kept the superpowers from direct war, but it also encouraged competition in technology, the space race and the proxy conflicts around the world. The arms race was therefore both a cause of tension and a means of managing it.

The Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962 showed the danger of the nuclear arms race. The Soviet decision to place missiles in Cuba and the American blockade brought the superpowers to the brink of war, and it convinced both sides that stability required restraint. The Partial Test Ban Treaty of 1963 and the Non-Proliferation Treaty of 1968 were responses to this danger, and they showed that the arms race could be managed through agreement.

The arms race also shaped the superpowers' budgets and their domestic politics. Both sides devoted large resources to missiles, submarines and bombers, and the competition encouraged the development of multiple independent warheads. The Strategic Arms Limitation Talks produced SALT I in 1972, which limited the number of launchers and paired with the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty. SALT II was signed in 1979 but was not ratified after the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan. Each agreement revealed the difficulty of limiting weapons that were tied to military and political strategies.

The space race was closely linked to the arms race. Sputnik in 1957 and the Apollo 11 landing in 1969 demonstrated the technological competition, and the missile programs that launched satellites were also capable of delivering nuclear warheads. The space race therefore intensified the arms race and kept the superpowers focused on technological superiority.

In the 1980s, the arms race reached a new phase. President Reagan's Strategic Defense Initiative, announced in 1983, aimed to protect the United States from missile attack, and the Soviet Union saw it as a threat to deterrence and an extension of the arms race into space. The Soviets faced economic strain from matching American spending, and this pressure contributed to Gorbachev's decision to negotiate. The Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty of 1987 was the first to eliminate a whole category of nuclear missiles, and it marked a change in the Cold War.

The arms race also affected the superpowers' relations with their allies and with the developing world. Both sides supplied weapons to client states, and the nuclear competition encouraged the expansion of alliance systems such as NATO and the Warsaw Pact. Nuclear weapons became a symbol of national prestige and political seriousness, which made it harder for either side to accept inferiority. The arms race reinforced the bipolar structure of the Cold War and limited the scope for compromise, even as both sides recognised the dangers it posed.

The arms race also changed the pace and character of the Cold War. Technologies such as multiple independent warheads, satellite reconnaissance and submarine-launched missiles made arms control more complicated, because each side had to verify what the other was doing. Verification became a central issue in the negotiations, and this created new forms of cooperation between the superpowers even as their rivalry continued. The arms race shaped not only the weapons themselves but also the relationship that developed between the two sides.

In conclusion, the arms race shaped the Cold War from 1962 to 1991 by sustaining nuclear deterrence, driving the space race and the search for arms control, and by imposing heavy economic costs on the Soviet Union. It did not cause the end of the Cold War on its own, but it created the conditions in which Gorbachev could seek agreement.

sampleAnswers.answer: The arms race shaped the Cold War by increasing the number of nuclear weapons held by both superpowers. The Cuban Missile Crisis in 1962 showed how dangerous the rivalry was, and it led to some restraint. Agreements such as the Partial Test Ban Treaty and the Non-Proliferation Treaty were signed. The space race was also part of the competition, with the Apollo 11 landing in 1969 showing American technological achievement. In 1972 the superpowers signed SALT I, which limited missiles. However, the arms race continued, and in the 1980s President Reagan announced the Strategic Defense Initiative. The Soviet Union was under economic pressure from the cost of competing, and this helped lead to arms control in the late 1980s. The arms race also had economic effects. Both superpowers devoted large shares of their budgets to weapons, and the Soviet economy in particular struggled to sustain the burden while producing consumer goods. The American defence build-up of the 1980s put further pressure on the Soviet leadership, which had to decide whether to keep matching American spending or to seek agreement. These economic realities help to explain why the arms race moved from confrontation towards negotiation in the late 1980s. sampleAnswers.answer:
Détente contributed to the end of the Cold War in an indirect way. It lowered tension, created channels of negotiation and exposed the Soviet bloc to Western ideas, but it did not end the rivalry on its own. The collapse of détente after 1979 and the reforms of Gorbachev were the more direct causes. The judgement is that détente helped create the conditions for change, but it was the Soviet Union's internal crisis and Gorbachev's decision to reform that ended the Cold War.

Détente produced real achievements. The Strategic Arms Limitation Talks led to SALT I in 1972, which limited the number of anti-ballistic missile systems and placed limits on offensive missiles. The Helsinki Accords of 1975 recognised the post-war borders of Europe and included commitments on human rights. These agreements gave Western governments a basis for pressing Soviet governments on human rights, and they encouraged dissidents in Eastern Europe to demand that their governments honour the commitments they had signed.

The Helsinki Accords also had an unintended effect. Dissident groups in Czechoslovakia, Poland and the Soviet Union used the human rights commitments to organise and to document abuses. This did not bring down communist governments by 1980, but it created a network of people who would later lead opposition. In this way détente contributed to the erosion of the Soviet bloc, even though it was intended to stabilise it.

However, détente was fragile. The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in December 1979 ended the mood of cooperation, and the United States responded by withdrawing support for SALT II and boycotting the Moscow Olympics in 1980. Relations returned to confrontation under Reagan, who increased defence spending and proposed the Strategic Defense Initiative in 1983. The collapse of détente shows that it had not resolved the underlying rivalry, so it could not by itself end the Cold War.

The Soviet Union's economic problems were more decisive. The war in Afghanistan was costly, and the economy was stagnating under the weight of military spending. Gorbachev, who came to power in 1985, introduced glasnost and perestroika to address these problems. His willingness to accept arms control, including the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty of 1987, and his refusal to use force to hold Eastern Europe, allowed the revolutions of 1989 to succeed. The fall of the Berlin Wall in November 1989 symbolised this change.

Détente also shaped the way Gorbachev could act. The arms control agreements of the 1970s had established a framework within which the superpowers negotiated, and the habit of talking made the later agreements possible. Without the earlier structure of negotiation, it is hard to see how reform could have been managed peacefully. Détente therefore contributed to the end of the Cold War as a precondition for later change, rather than as its direct cause.

The Reagan administration combined a military build-up with offers of arms reduction, and this changed the Cold War. The Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty of 1987 eliminated a whole class of missiles, showing that pressure and negotiation could work together. The Soviet economy, weakened by the cost of Afghanistan and by falling oil revenue after 1985, was less able to sustain the military competition that Reagan's policies intensified.

In conclusion, détente contributed to the end of the Cold War, but only to a limited extent. It built channels for negotiation, supported human rights in the Eastern bloc and established a framework for later arms control. However, its collapse after 1979 shows that it did not resolve the rivalry, and the decisive changes came from the Soviet economic crisis and Gorbachev's reforms. Détente was therefore an important foundation for the end of the Cold War, but not its main cause.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 21–25 row: a clear judgement that détente contributed indirectly, supported by SALT, Helsinki, the collapse after Afghanistan and Gorbachev's reforms. It would lift further by weighing the Helsinki effect on dissidents against the economic causes more precisely.

The Helsinki Accords of 1975 recognised the borders of Europe and included human rights commitments, which dissidents in the Soviet bloc later used to press their governments.

However, détente collapsed after the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979. Reagan increased defence spending and relations returned to confrontation. The decisive change came when Gorbachev introduced glasnost and perestroika after 1985, accepted arms control and refused to use force in Eastern Europe. The revolutions of 1989 and the fall of the Berlin Wall followed.

Détente also had economic dimensions. Trade expanded, American grain sales to the Soviet Union grew, and Western banks lent to the Soviet bloc. These links made the later economic crisis more damaging for the Soviet Union, but they also showed that détente rested on a weak economic base.

Détente was therefore an important background to the end of the Cold War, but Gorbachev's reforms were more significant.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Economic and political developments were the most important influence on the emergence of détente between 1969 and 1979, although the nuclear balance and the war in Vietnam also made the superpowers willing to reduce tensions. Both superpowers faced problems that made confrontation expensive, and the leaders of the United States and the Soviet Union responded by seeking agreements on arms control and trade. The assessment must weigh the economic and political developments against these other influences, and it must recognise that détente's impact was real but limited.

The economic and political developments that favoured détente were significant. The United States faced rising inflation, a growing balance of payments deficit and the cost of the Vietnam War, and President Nixon suspended the convertibility of the dollar into gold in August 1971. The Soviet economy was growing more slowly, and Moscow needed Western technology and grain. The 1972 agreement to sell American grain to the Soviet Union illustrated how economic need encouraged both sides to trade. Politically, the Sino-American opening of February 1972 gave Nixon leverage over Moscow, and the Soviet leadership wanted to prevent a China and United States alignment.

The nuclear balance reinforced these developments. By the early 1970s both superpowers had large arsenals, and the Anti-Ballistic Missile treaty and the interim agreement known as SALT I, signed in May 1972, reflected a shared interest in limiting costly competition. These agreements were partly a response to economic pressure, because each side wished to reduce defence spending, but they also recognised that neither superpower could gain a decisive advantage through an arms race.

The war in Vietnam was another influence. American public opinion and Congress turned against the war, and this made Nixon eager for negotiations that would reduce the Soviet Union's willingness to support North Vietnam. The Soviet leadership, for its part, feared the consequences of a confrontation and wanted stable relations with the West. The Ostpolitik policy of West Germany, which led to the Treaty of Moscow in 1970, also reduced tension in Europe and made Soviet leaders more confident of gaining benefits from diplomacy.

The impact of détente was real but limited. The Helsinki Accords of 1975 gave the Soviet Union recognition of its European borders, while committing it to human rights provisions that it did not fully implement. Détente reduced the risk of nuclear war and produced trade and arms control agreements, but it did not end ideological rivalry or regional conflicts. The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in December 1979 showed how fragile the relationship was.

Critics in both countries limited détente. Conservatives in the United States argued that the agreements left the Soviet Union with advantages, and the Jackson–Vanik amendment of 1974 linked trade to Soviet emigration policy, which Moscow regarded as interference. In the Soviet Union, leaders continued to support revolutionary movements in Africa and Asia, which Washington saw as a breach of the spirit of détente. These disputes show that economic and political developments encouraged cooperation without removing the underlying rivalry between the two systems.

On balance, economic and political developments were the most important influence on the emergence of détente, because they gave both superpowers a practical interest in limiting confrontation. The nuclear balance and Vietnam created pressure in the same direction. Détente was therefore a product of changing circumstances rather than a fundamental change in the rivalry between the two systems. Its limits were shown by how quickly it collapsed once the conditions that had supported it began to change after 1979. The Helsinki Accords, for all their limits, also gave dissidents in Eastern Europe a document to invoke, which made human rights a lasting part of the East–West relationship.

To lift it further, examine more closely why the economic pressures on each superpower differed.

Détente had some success, but it did not end the Cold War. The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979 brought it to an end, and tensions rose again after that.

A stronger response would weigh the economic and political developments against the other influences. The nuclear balance gave both sides reasons to limit competition through SALT I, and the Sino-American opening reduced the Soviet Union's strategic options. These connections show why détente was a product of several pressures, not one, and why its impact had clear limits.

sampleAnswers.answer:
A shift towards détente during the Cold War came from the pressures on both superpowers in the late 1960s. Détente, meaning a relaxation of tension, was not a reconciliation of ideologies or an end to rivalry. It was an attempt by the United States and the Soviet Union to manage their competition, limit the dangers of nuclear war and secure advantages without a direct conflict. Its appeal was strongest in Washington and Moscow after the crises of the 1960s, when the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962 had shown how close the two powers had come to nuclear war.

The most important pressure in the United States was the war in Vietnam. The conflict had consumed American resources and political support from the mid-1960s, and by 1969 it was clear that the United States could not win it on acceptable terms. Richard Nixon and his national security adviser, Henry Kissinger, sought a way out of the war and a way to strengthen American bargaining power. Improving relations with the Soviet Union and opening contact with China offered the prospect of leverage over Hanoi and over Moscow. The Sino-Soviet split, which had grown from the late 1950s, gave Washington an opportunity to play the two communist powers against each other.

The Soviet Union also had strong reasons to seek détente. Its economy was slowing, and it faced a costly military build-up that drained resources from civilian development. Leonid Brezhnev wanted recognition of the USSR as a superpower equal to the United States, and he hoped to secure Western technology and trade. Both sides were also drawn to the principle of mutual deterrence. The development of nuclear arsenals meant that each could destroy the other, and the doctrine of mutually assured destruction made limiting the arms race a shared interest.

Détente produced concrete results. The Strategic Arms Limitation Talks led to the SALT I agreements, signed in Moscow in May 1972, which limited anti-ballistic missile systems and placed limits on offensive missile launchers. The Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty was part of the same package. Nixon’s visit to China in February 1972 and the Helsinki Accords of 1975, which recognised post-war borders in Europe and included human rights commitments, showed that détente could extend beyond arms control. Trade expanded, and both sides agreed to reduce the risk of accidental war.

The limits of détente were also clear. Each superpower continued to support its allies in the developing world, and the Soviet Union sent forces into Afghanistan in 1979, which ended the period of relaxed relations. Critics in the United States argued that détente had given the Soviet Union advantages in weapons without enough reciprocal concessions. Nonetheless, détente had reduced the threat of nuclear confrontation and created a framework of talks that later agreements would build upon.

The détente period also reflected changes in the superpower relationship. By the early 1970s both sides had reached a rough nuclear balance, and each recognised that a new arms race would be costly. The superpowers found common ground in limiting missile defences and in agreeing rules for managing crises. This was not an agreement on ideology, but a recognition that both sides had an interest in predictable competition.

In conclusion, a shift towards détente was driven by the costs of the Vietnam War, the strains of the Sino-Soviet split, the Soviet Union’s economic and military pressures and the shared fear of nuclear destruction. It did not end the Cold War, but it made the superpowers more willing to negotiate, and it set the pattern for the arms control agreements of the 1970s and 1980s.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 21–25 row: the answer makes a sustained judgement that shared pressures, not only American weakness, drove détente, and it supports this with dated evidence. To go further, it could assess the limits of détente more critically against the evidence it gives.

sampleAnswers.answer:
A shift towards détente happened because both superpowers faced costs from the Cold War. The United States was struggling in Vietnam, and Nixon wanted to negotiate from strength. The Soviet Union faced a slowing economy and the cost of its military build-up. Both sides also feared nuclear destruction, and the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962 had shown how close the two powers had come to war.

Nixon and Kissinger saw détente as a way to gain leverage. Opening contact with China in February 1972 and negotiating with Moscow allowed the United States to play the communist powers against each other, and the Sino-Soviet split made this possible. The SALT I agreements, signed in May 1972, limited anti-ballistic missile systems and placed limits on offensive missiles, which showed that the two sides were willing to accept restraints.

The Soviet Union also wanted détente. Brezhnev hoped to secure Western technology and trade and to be recognised as a superpower equal to the United States. The doctrine of mutually assured destruction meant that each side had a shared interest in limiting the arms race, even though rivalry continued.

Nixon’s policy of linkage tied progress on arms control to Soviet behaviour in the Middle East and Vietnam. Kissinger argued that the superpowers should negotiate from a position of strength, and that détente could be used to restrain Soviet actions. This approach made détente a strategic tool rather than a policy of goodwill. Public support for détente in the United States was weak, and critics argued that the agreements favoured Moscow.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Gorbachev's policies made a very large contribution to the end of the Cold War, because they removed the Soviet Union's willingness to use force to keep its empire in Eastern Europe and reduced the military confrontation with the United States. But his policies were not the sole cause. The Soviet economy was failing, Reagan's military build-up had raised the costs of competition, and nationalist movements across the Soviet bloc were already growing. Gorbachev's reforms were intended to renew the Soviet system rather than end the Cold War, and their unintended consequences proved decisive.

Gorbachev came to power in March 1985 determined to revive a stagnant economy. Perestroika introduced limited market elements into state enterprises, and glasnost allowed open criticism of the party and its history. These reforms were intended to strengthen Soviet socialism, but they weakened the party's control over information and debate. Glasnost in particular gave nationalist and dissident groups a public voice in the Baltic republics, Ukraine and Eastern Europe, which made it harder for Moscow to suppress them when they challenged communist rule.

Gorbachev's foreign policy went further. His new political thinking accepted that Soviet security did not depend on controlling its neighbours, and it made arms control possible. At Reykjavik in October 1986 the two leaders came close to eliminating nuclear weapons, and the INF Treaty of December 1987 removed a whole category of missiles. The decision to withdraw from Afghanistan, agreed in 1988 and completed in February 1989, ended a costly war that had symbolised the Brezhnev era. In December 1988 Gorbachev announced unilateral troop reductions and implicitly renounced the Brezhnev Doctrine, under which the Soviet Union had invaded Czechoslovakia in 1968.

The test of these policies came in 1989. When revolutions spread through Poland and Hungary, the Soviet Union did not intervene as it had in Hungary in 1956 and Czechoslovakia in 1968. Poland's Solidarity formed a government in August 1989, and Hungary opened its border with Austria in September. The Berlin Wall fell on 9 November, and by the end of the year the communist governments of Czechoslovakia, Bulgaria and Romania had fallen. Gorbachev's refusal to use force was the decisive factor in allowing these revolutions to succeed, and it made the Cold War's division of Europe untenable.

Other factors weighed as heavily. Reagan's missile defence programme of 1983 and sustained American military spending raised the Soviet Union's costs, and the economic decline of the 1980s, including the collapse in oil prices in 1986, left Moscow unable to sustain the arms race. Nationalist movements in the Soviet republics and Eastern Europe would probably have pressed for change regardless of Gorbachev, and his reforms did not produce the outcome he intended. By 1991 he had lost control of the process, and the failed August coup and the dissolution of the USSR in December 1991 were consequences his policies had released rather than planned.

On balance, Gorbachev's policies contributed to the end of the Cold War to a very great extent, because they removed the Soviet willingness to defend its position in Eastern Europe and allowed German reunification within NATO in October 1990. Yet the end of the Cold War was also the product of pressures that predated him, and the collapse of the Soviet state was partly a consequence of reforms he had not foreseen. His policies were a necessary condition for the end of the Cold War rather than a sufficient one.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 21–25 row with a sustained judgement that separates Gorbachev's deliberate foreign policy from the broader pressures on the Soviet system and weighs them against each other. The evidence is specific (Reykjavik, the INF Treaty, the 1989 revolutions), and the final judgement is precise about what kind of cause his policies were. The argument would be stronger if the economic evidence were linked to a specific Soviet decision.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Gorbachev's policies contributed a great deal to the end of the Cold War. When he came to power in 1985 he introduced perestroika, which was an attempt to reform the Soviet economy, and glasnost, which meant more openness in Soviet society. These policies gave people more freedom to speak, and they made it harder for the government to control dissent. Gorbachev also wanted to improve relations with the West, so he worked with President Reagan on arms control.

The two leaders met at Reykjavik in 1986, and the INF Treaty was signed in 1987. This treaty removed a whole group of nuclear missiles from Europe. Gorbachev also withdrew Soviet troops from Afghanistan, which had been a costly war for the Soviet Union. These actions helped to reduce tension between the superpowers and showed that the Soviet Union wanted a different relationship with the West.

In Eastern Europe, Gorbachev did not use force to stop protests. In 1989 many countries in Eastern Europe changed their governments, and the Berlin Wall came down in November. This was a major change, because the Soviet Union had used force to crush rebellions in Hungary in 1956 and Czechoslovakia in 1968. Gorbachev's decision not to intervene allowed these changes to happen, which was a turning point for the whole Cold War order.

However, other factors were also important. The United States spent a great deal on defence under Reagan, and the Soviet economy was in serious trouble. Gorbachev's reforms were not meant to end the Soviet Union, but the Soviet Union did break up in 1991, so the results went far beyond what he planned. His policies were therefore important, but other factors also helped to end the Cold War.

The weighing of other factors is brief and the judgement restates the opening, so it does not sustain the argument, and it lacks the historical terms of a top answer.
